A new documentary "All of Us" has landed on Apple TV, telling the story of how a public primary school uses a unique approach to educate students with different needs.

iPhone and iPad play a key role in what is being hailed as a model of inclusive education, enabling every child to benefit……

Students who need extra support due to disabilities are often taught separately from mainstream students. The traditional view is that putting everyone in the same classroom disrupts the learning of most students.

Ruby Bridges Elementary has a different take, and the results prove that inclusive teaching is not a disruption at all — it actually helps all students academically and socially. The results were so remarkable that the school's principal and a kindergarten teacher were both named Principal of the Year and Teacher of the Year in 2025.

A 70-minute documentary is now streaming on Apple TV, telling the story of a school that "breaks the mould".

At Ruby Bridges, all students learn together in regular classrooms. Every child does maths together, reads together, and sings together in music class. Teachers and specialists work closely side by side in the classroom, and the results speak for themselves. So how do they do it? Ruby Bridges is a public school — it does not receive extra funding or additional staff for this. There is no magic solution either. It simply comes down to a group of educators who decided to stop separating children and chose to put their faith in the power of learning together. This is the story of a school that breaks the mould — a school that is unique, but really should not be unique.

iPad and iPhone play a key role

Some students have severe communication difficulties, and the Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) software running on iPad and iPhone has made a dramatic difference in their ability to communicate with teachers and classmates.

One major finding is that AAC apps are not only useful for students with communication difficulties — they help every student. Founding principal Cathi Davis told me:

Whether a student has stronger reading and language skills, or is at the very beginning of learning to communicate or use language, they can all use AAC tools to generate, expand, or express ideas, and they participate at a high level. With this ever-present communication support, we can overcome challenges with handwriting and writing endurance, and even reduce the anxiety of speaking up loudly, while breaking down barriers that sometimes appear in the classroom or in life……

As the documentary reveals, this model of teaching is not only effective for students with additional needs — it benefits all students. That point is indisputable. A dedicated website for the documentary also offers a comprehensive set of video resources for other schools that want to follow in Ruby Bridges' footsteps.
